ann_28.text: This part acts on only 8 of 242 training patients (3%), women whose chest pain is brought on by exercise; 7 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 62-year-old woman with chest pain on exercise, a normal resting ECG, a flat ST segment and resting blood pressure of 145 mm Hg), it raises the predicted risk from about 12% to about 92% (the model has little data on this; on the training data only).
Through it, chest pain brought on by exercise clearly raises that patient's predicted risk from about 12% to about 92%.

Through it, being a woman rather than a man raises that patient's predicted risk from about 12% to about 92%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG lower it from about 92% to about 12% (on the training data only).

Across the whole model, being a woman clearly lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy (from about 33% to about 1%, against about 23% to about 1% otherwise).
Being a woman lowers it slightly more if exercise does not bring on chest pain, and chest pain on exercise raises it only slightly, and only if the resting ECG shows no left ventricular hypertrophy.

ann_29.text: This part barely changes the predictions.
Through it, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG raise a typical patient's predicted risk only slightly, from about 23% to about 24% (on the training data only).

ann_30.text: This part acts on 111 of 242 training patients (46%), all of them patients with a flat ST segment; 72 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with a flat ST segment, 1.2 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG and a reversible thallium defect), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 96% to about 97% (on the training data only).
Through it, a flat ST segment raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 23% to about 29% (on the training data only).
The rise from a flat ST segment is only slightly larger if exercise brings on chest pain (on the training data only).
Being a woman and the resting ECG change the predicted risk only slightly through this part (on the training data only).

ann_31.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 1%), non-anginal chest pain (about 2%) or atypical angina (about 12%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 23%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 23% to about 96%, a flat ST segment raises it to about 80%, a reversible thallium defect to about 47%, and more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) from about 16% to about 50% (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) raises it from about 13% to about 45%, older age (42 to 66 years) from about 17% to about 28%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG from about 23% to about 33% (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it from about 23% to about 1%, and a fixed defect on the thallium scan to about 8% (15 patients; the model has little data on this), both on the training data only.
Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL (to about 19%) and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute (from about 26% to about 21%) lower it only slightly (on the training data only).
It ignores resting blood pressure.

ann_28.original: Hypothesis: node 665 is a three-way AND gate that fires only for women (sex:0 set) with exercise-induced angina (exang:0 unset, i.e. exang=yes) and no left-ventricular hypertrophy on resting ECG (restecg:2 unset). The restecg:2 chain 2349 -> 2771 never leaves the ReLU linear region on standardized one-hot inputs (2349 in [1.15,3.11], 2771 in [1.99,3.72]), so the gate collapses exactly to relu(1.41 sex:0 - 1.71 exang:0 - 1.18 restecg:2 - 3.39). Evidence (train, n=242): pre-activation max is 2.117, reached only when all three conditions hold; removing any one condition drives it negative (no female: -0.86; no exang: -2.53; LVH present: -0.24). The gate is active on 8/242 rows (3.3%), always at the single value 2.117, and 7 of those 8 are positive cases. Closed form matches the forward pass (check_explanation closed-form err 0.0049, numeric err 0).
ann_28.proposed: A part that acts only on 8 women whose chest pain is brought on by exercise and raises their predicted risk from about 12% to about 92%; signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG switch it off.

ann_29.original: Hypothesis: node 2447 is an always-active affine relay of restecg:2 (LVH on resting ECG). Evidence (train): pre-activation in [0.485, 2.516], so the ReLU never clips; through its 0.026 output weight it adds 0.026*1.02 = 0.026 per SD of restecg:2 to the logit (logit-term SD 0.026 vs total logit SD 4.3), i.e. it is practically inert and simply nudges the direct restecg:2 weight from 0.224 to 0.250. Closed-form err 0.0083 (3-s.f. rounding).
ann_29.proposed: A part that barely changes the predictions; signs of left ventricular hypertrophy raise the risk only slightly through it.

ann_30.original: Hypothesis: serial composition H(G(sex:0, exang:0, restecg:2), slope:2). Node 3598 = relu(1.51 slope:2 + 1.05 G - 0.76) and node 1650 = relu(1.29 G + 1.31*3598 - 0.73). Because G takes only the values 0 or 2.117 and slope:2 is binary, 1650 has exactly four regimes on train: G=0 & slope not flat -> 0 (n=131, 27% positive); G=0 & flat slope (slope:2) -> 0.446 (n=103, 63% positive); G on & slope not flat -> 2.097 (n=1, negative); G on & flat slope -> 6.092 (n=7, all positive). So without the gate it is a small additional flat-ST-slope bonus (+0.34 logit after the 0.772 output weight, on top of the direct slope:2 weight); with the gate it amplifies the female-exertional-angina signal, and the flat-slope ReLU 3598 makes the two conditions super-additive (6.09 vs 0.45+2.10). Evidence: activation_profile on node 1650 (train): active 45.9%, mean 0.375, SD 1.018, max 6.092; values confirmed by local forward pass.
ann_30.proposed: A part that acts on patients with a flat ST segment and raises their predicted risk; only slightly for the typical patient it acts on.

ann_31.original: Hypothesis: additive composition. The logit z of node 0 is a linear score over 17 direct standardized inputs (dominated by ca 1.93, sex:1 1.67, cp:4 1.21, slope:2 1.05, chol 0.72, oldpeak 0.71) plus 0.772 x flat_slope_amplifier plus 0.026 x restecg2_relay; 7 inputs (trestbps, fbs:0, restecg:0, restecg:1, exang:1, thal:3, thal:4) are disconnected. get_formula shows node 0 as ReLU, but for this binary task the model output is sigmoid(z) on the pre-activation (compute_performance train AUC 0.945 equals AUC of z; sigmoid(relu(z)) would give 0.912). Evidence (train, n=242, local forward passes): direct-linear logit SD 4.33 vs amplifier term SD 0.79 vs relay term SD 0.026. Dropping the amplifier term lowers train AUC 0.945 -> 0.930 and accuracy 0.888 -> 0.868; the direct linear part alone gives AUC 0.931. So the network is essentially logistic regression plus one sparse nonlinear correction: a flat-slope bonus (+0.34 logit) and a large boost (+4.7 logit) for the 7 women with exertional angina, no LVH and flat ST slope. Kernel SHAP on the full model (train) ranks ca 0.149, sex:1 0.130, slope:2 0.121, cp:4 0.116, oldpeak 0.049, thal:7 0.046, chol 0.044 (mean |SHAP| on probability). Function preservation after the two input splits: max abs err 1.8e-15.
ann_31.proposed: Typical angina, non-anginal chest pain and atypical angina lower the predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms. More vessels coloured, a flat ST segment, more ST depression, a reversible thallium defect, higher cholesterol, older age and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy raise it; being a woman lowers it. The model ignores resting blood pressure.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk about 23%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 1%), non-anginal chest pain (about 2%) or atypical angina (about 12%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 23% to about 96%, and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment at peak exercise raises it to about 80% (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy: for a typical patient it clearly falls from about 33% to about 1% with those signs, and from about 23% to about 1% without them.
More ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises the predicted risk from about 16% to about 50%, and higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 13% to about 45% (on the training data only).

One small part acts only on 8 training patients, women whose chest pain is brought on by exercise, and raises their predicted risk from about 12% to about 92% (the model has little data on this; on the training data only).

Worth checking: patients with typical angina get the lowest predicted risk of all chest pain types, below patients with no chest pain symptoms.
Worth checking: the model treats a fixed defect on the thallium scan as lowering the risk compared with other scan results apart from a reversible defect, from only 15 training patients.

worth_checking.flag: rare category drives a large effect
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: one part raises the predicted risk from about 12% to about 92% for 8 training patients, women whose chest pain is brought on by exercise.

worth_checking.flag: exercise-induced angina matters only with normal resting ECG
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: in that part, chest pain on exercise raises the risk only for patients without signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG, and those signs lower the predicted risk there.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

values.fbs: fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_28.text: This part acts on 8 of 242 training patients (3%); nearly all of them are women and patients whose chest pain is brought on by exercise.

For a typical patient it acts on, it raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% without this part to about 92% with it (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 8 training patients (patients the part acts on).
In the training data, 7 of these 8 patients had heart disease.

The model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man, and even more so if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 33% to about 1% if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy, and from about 23% to about 1% if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG.

The model gives a slightly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 23% to about 1% if exercise does not bring on chest pain, and from about 23% to about 4% if exercise brings on chest pain.

This changes the prediction only slightly: for a typical patient, going from no chest pain on exercise to chest pain brought on by exercise moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 23% to about 23% if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG, and from about 33% to about 33% if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a clearly higher predicted risk of heart disease if exercise brings on chest pain (about 92%) than if exercise does not bring on chest pain (about 12%).

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy (about 12%) than if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG (about 92%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 92%) than if the patient is a man (about 12%) (on the training data only).

ann_29.text: Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy (about 24%) than if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG (about 23%) (on the training data only).
This part barely changes the model's predictions (by at most 0.7 percentage points).

ann_30.text: This part acts on 111 of 242 training patients (46%); nearly all of them are patients with a flat ST segment.
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 96% without this part to about 97% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 72 of these 111 patients had heart disease.

The model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise than if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than a flat ST segment, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from slope of the ST segment at peak exercise other than a flat ST segment to a flat ST segment moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 23% to about 80% if exercise brings on chest pain, and from about 23% to about 80% if exercise does not bring on chest pain (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 29%) than if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than a flat ST segment (about 23%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if exercise brings on chest pain (about 97%) than if exercise does not bring on chest pain (about 97%).

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy (about 97%) than if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG (about 97%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 97%) than if the patient is a man (about 97%) (on the training data only).

ann_31.text: For a typical patient, number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy going from 0 vessels to 2 vessels raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 23% to about 96% (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 80%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 23%) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, ST depression on exercise going from 0.0 mm to 2.8 mm raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 16% to about 50% (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, serum cholesterol going from 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 13% to about 45% (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect (about 47%) than if thallium stress test result is something other than a fixed defect on the thallium scan, a reversible defect on the thallium scan (about 23%) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 1%) than if the patient is a man (about 23%) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 1%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 23%).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has non-anginal chest pain (about 2%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 23%).

For a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a fixed defect (about 8%) than if thallium stress test result is something other than a fixed defect on the thallium scan, a reversible defect on the thallium scan (about 23%) (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).
For a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 17% to about 28% (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has atypical angina (about 12%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 23%).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy (about 33%) than if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG (about 23%) (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, maximum heart rate going from 118 beats per minute to 175 beats per minute slightly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease from about 26% to about 21% (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment slopes down at peak exercise (about 27%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 23%) (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).

For a typical patient, the model gives a slightly lower predicted risk of heart disease if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL (about 19%) than if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less (about 23%) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, the model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if exercise brings on chest pain (about 23%) than if exercise does not bring on chest pain (about 23%).
It ignores resting blood pressure.

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 80%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 23%) (on the training data only).
For a typical patient, ST depression on exercise going from 0.0 mm to 2.8 mm raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 16% to about 50% (on the training data only).

The model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man, and even more so if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 33% to about 1% if the resting ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy, and from about 23% to about 1% if resting ECG is something other than signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG.

The model gives a slightly higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise than if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than a flat ST segment, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from slope of the ST segment at peak exercise other than a flat ST segment to a flat ST segment moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 23% to about 80% if exercise brings on chest pain, and from about 23% to about 80% if exercise does not bring on chest pain (on the training data only).
The model ignores resting blood pressure.
